title: The Peculiar Pebble of Market Day
markdown:
Wizard Cedric lived in a village tucked beside a secret shimmering tarn in the Whispering Peaks of Aeridor, where paths wore switchbacks like a mountain goat’s trail and cottages clung like moss. He was a wizard of particular habits — some said too particular. Spectacles polished thrice before breakfast. Spell ingredients alphabetical. Enchantments on his market stall always double-checked. The cottage smelled of dried herbs and warm beeswax, a haven of quiet order. Lentil, a cat as sleek as midnight with eyes like polished emeralds, moved through that order like a shadow, her tail a silent story of the house’s mood.

Market Day. Grey robes freshly pressed, a basket of herbs that shimmered with a violet so deep it seemed to swallow light, Cedric padded toward his usual spot by the chattering town fountain. Lentil trotted beside him, tail flicking excitement and slow thought in a rhythm only he understood.

“Now, Lentil. This stall must be perfect. Mistress Gable’s prize-winning jam depends on these moon-petal herbs. They must be… oh, dear.”

One moon-petal drooped, delicate purple flowers wilted as if they had heard woeful news. A tremor through Cedric’s whiskers. Not perfection. An insult to market-readiness.

“A wilting herb. Unacceptable. It needs verve.”

His hand fumbled for a tiny vial of Verdant Vigor, a bubbly concoction designed to perk even a glum daisy. He whispered words as precise as a snowflake’s edges. A faint hopeful green pulsed from his fingertips.

The potion, eager to spread cheer, did not land on the herb. With astonishing accuracy it zipped past and struck a small grey pebble lying innocently near the stall — overlooked in the weekly tidy-up.

Poof.

The pebble pulsed intense emerald, then grew. Astonishingly fast. Robin’s egg to goose egg to melon, pushing against neatly arranged jars of dried pixie dust. Cedric’s mouth hung open. Lentil, grooming a paw with fastidious care, paused mid-lick, one emerald ear swiveling toward the burgeoning boulder.

“Oh, bother.” The pebble, now a prize-winning pumpkin, nudged his jars and let out a soft rumbling hum.

Cedric’s meticulous nature wrestled with the unfolding silliness. The market was waking; cheerful chatter tinged with puzzled murmuring. People pointed. The pebble, still glowing persistent green, settled firmly in the middle of the path.

“Perhaps a minor charm to shrink it? Or levitation to tuck it out of the way?” He fingered a smooth crystal, ready to cast.

Lentil, with a decisive flick that spoke volumes of feline wisdom, nudged his boot. The market called. Herbs needed selling. A peculiar pebble was not going to stop Market Day. He could not fuss when the stall needed minding.

With a sigh that ruffled his neatly trimmed beard, Cedric slipped the rumbling glowing pebble into his pocket. Surprisingly warm, like a freshly baked scone. He plastered on the smile reserved for indecisive customers. “Good morning! Lovely day for Market Day!”

All eyes, and all whispers, were on the bulging pocket.

High above the hamlet, where air was thin and clouds snagged on jagged peaks like sheep’s wool on brambles, lived Fizzwick: a dragon of considerable age and even more considerable desire for peace. He detested fuss. Loud noises, sudden movements, anything that disturbed his afternoon nap sent him into a silent simmering huff that could melt icicles at fifty paces.

On his favourite sun-warmed crag, enjoying a particularly quiet stretch of sunlight, he felt an unusual tremor. Not an earthquake. A growing tremor. And a faint insistent green glow that seemed to seep into his thoughts.

“Hmph.” Smoky breath stirred pine needles. “More commotion. Just what the world needs. A bright, noisy, growing thing.”

Back at the market, the pebble staged a performance. It grew to the size of a small cart, blocking the path people needed to reach baker and cheese seller. It pulsed with a strangely soothing light that made shoppers pause, smile vaguely, and forget why they were there. Mistress Gable, clutching plump berries, giggled and patted it as if it were a very friendly unusually large pet.

Cedric, flustered beyond reasonable wizardly composure, tried a Dimming Charm. He pictured shrinking, fading, pebble-sized again. Words, a wisp of smoke into his own face, an explosive sneeze. The pebble pulsed brighter. A tiny sprout of bright green moss appeared on its surface, waving like a flag of defiance.

Lentil watched from beneath the stall, green eyes reflecting glow with an almost mischievous gleam. She stretched, yawned a delicate pink tongue, and with a silent elegant leap landed atop the pebble. She sat there, a small dark silhouette against shimmering green, as if it were her personal, slightly inconvenient, throne.

Undeterred by moss, Cedric tried a Stasis Spell, hoping to freeze growth. He imagined unchanging. The spell only made the pebble vibrate like a happy bumblebee. A nearby stall of delicate glass ornaments tinkled and chimed wildly.

“Oh, my stars and garters!” He abandoned the herbs to steady the teetering display.

Growth continued, relentless. A substantial rolling obstacle, nudging the base of the town’s beloved moss-covered fountain. The fountain, with its chipped cherub, had stood for generations. Cold dread. This was more than peculiar. A genuine problem. He had intended to sell herbs, not create a town-wide obstruction.

High above, Fizzwick’s patience wore thinner than spider silk. The insistent soothing glow had reached his cave, seeping under the door, disrupting afternoon meditations. Distant muffled sounds of market-goers being far too happy about being inconvenienced. Collective gentle apathy. It drove him mad.

“This is absurd.” He unfolded vast wings with a sigh like wind in a canyon. “All this fuss.”

The pebble, cart-sized, blocked the main path, light making everyone too content to move, too happy to notice the fountain’s groan. Cedric watched, dread chilling him more than any mountain gust. He had failed. A spell that worked too well on the wrong thing. A very large, very green, very round pickle.

He retreated behind the stall, damp earth and misplaced magic thick in the air. Overturned crate, head in hands, neatly pressed robes rumpled. Lentil hopped onto his lap, purring a soft rumble through his chest, a small beacon.

“It’s no good, Lentil. I prepared for everything. Weather. Customers. Every conceivable spell. Except this. A spell that works too well on the wrong thing. I’ve made a terrible mess.” He looked at the pebble pressing the fountain with a groan of ancient stone. “What am I going to do?”

Lentil’s purr stayed a steady anchor. A memory surfaced: the pebble’s light made people stop, smile, forget worries. Not aggressive magic. Gentle. Pervasive. Designed to soothe.

“Wait.” He stroked her fur, the familiar texture grounding him. “The spell wasn’t about forcing change. It was about enhancing. What if I don’t try to stop it? What if I use its own nature? What if I make it do what it’s already good at, for a different purpose?”

A seed of hope. He stood, movements no longer hesitant. Lentil jumped down, emerald eyes intent, silent understanding.

“We don’t need a counter-spell. We need a spell that makes people see what needs to be done, not just feel good about it.” He walked toward the humming pebble. Market-goers in its haze continued to hum and smile, oblivious.

He did not reach for a complicated incantation. He imagined the soothing light spreading, not to lull, but to make them aware: of the pebble, of the fountain, of the gentle nudge they needed to move, to act, to save the square. He hummed an old lullaby his grandmother used to sing, and directed intent not with force but with persuasion. The pebble pulsed. Light flared, not harshly, a soft encompassing warmth into every corner.

Shoppers blinked. The haze lifted as if a curtain had been pulled. They looked at the pebble, the wobbling fountain, each other. A collective gasp, then a flurry. People began to move, to push, to guide the pebble away from delicate stonework with renewed purpose.

A shadow fell over the square, so large it eclipsed midday sun. Fizzwick landed with a soft thump that nonetheless shook the ground, thoroughly annoyed.

“Honestly. All this fuss for a glowing rock? It’s ruining my nap.”

Before anyone could protest, Fizzwick, with a flick of his enormous snout, gave the pebble a gentle but firm nudge. Guided by that minimal effort and the townspeople’s concerted push, it rolled smoothly, picked up speed, and disappeared with a distant rumble into a deep moss-lined quarry nearby. Glow extinguished.

Commotion ceased. Silence, then the happy chatter of a relieved town and the gentle gurgle of the now-safe fountain. Cedric, no longer flustered, watched the market return to its lively hum: fresh bread, ripe fruit. His stall, with perfectly presentable herbs, was no longer the centre of attention, and that was perfectly all right. Lentil rubbed his legs, a purr sweeter than any spell. He scooped her up, burying his face in fur, cat and home. Smiling faces. A standing fountain. Warmth that had nothing to do with misplaced potions and everything to do with a community that had remembered how to push.

Mistress Gable bought her moon-petal herbs after all. The drooping one had perked up on its own, possibly from proximity to so much unintended vigour. Cedric did not double-check the stall a fourth time. Lentil’s tail, writing the house’s mood on the walk home, said the order could wait until after tea.
characters: Cedric (wizard), Lentil (cat), Fizzwick (dragon), Mistress Gable (jam maker)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
